pests.name: Parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar)
pests.symptoms_beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and yellow-orange dots, chewing the feathery leaves. They can strip a young plant, but on an established dill they usually do only light damage.
pests.cause_beginner: These are the caterpillars of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on dill and other carrot-family plants. They are also a welcome garden visitor, since they turn into a beautiful butterfly.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: On a big plant, just leave them; the damage is minor and you get butterflies. If they threaten a small planting, pick them off by hand and move them to a spare dill plant.
pests.prevention_beginner: Grow a little extra dill so there is enough to share with the caterpillars, and simply relocate them rather than spraying.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes), banded green, black, and yellow, feed on the foliage. On an established dill the defoliation is usually light and cosmetic; a heavy load can strip a seedling.
pests.cause_seasoned: Dill is a larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly. The caterpillars are a feature as much as a pest, so dill is often planted deliberately to support them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On established plants, tolerate them, the feeding is minor and the butterflies are a benefit; on small plantings, handpick and relocate to a sacrificial dill. Bt is effective if control is truly needed, but is rarely warranted on a host plant grown partly for the butterflies.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Manage by tolerance and a little surplus planting rather than control: grow enough dill to share, relocate larvae from plants you want to protect, and reserve sprays for genuine seedling threats.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of the feathery leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Dill's own flowers also draw in ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop used fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Dill's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on dill; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. Dill itself, allowed to flower, is a strong insectary that recruits aphid predators.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which dill's own umbel flowers attract.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting some dill flower draws in the aphid predators it is famous for hosting.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and flower stalks, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungal disease that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, crowding, and overwatering.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding and overhead watering. Most home crops are picked before it does much harm.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and water at the base rather than over the leaves.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most commonly noted fungal disease of dill, that builds in warm days with cool humid nights, in crowded stands, and where plants are overwatered; coated leaves lose quality.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe heraclei on Apiaceae), favored by warm days, cool humid nights, dense stands with poor airflow, and excess moisture. Utah State University notes dill mildews when overwatered.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering; the leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a tall plant held for seed is more exposed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen and overwatering, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for seed.

diseases.name: Leaf spot / leaf blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small tan to brown spots, sometimes with a yellow halo, that spread on the leaves and can merge until the leaflets wilt and die back, worst in wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread on wet leaves and splashing water and can arrive on infected seed. Spotted, blighted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, rotate the bed, and clear infected debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small tan-brown leaf lesions, sometimes yellow-haloed, that expand and coalesce until leaflets blight and die; favored by wet, splashy conditions and prolonged leaf wetness. Cercospora leaf blight (Cercosporidium punctum) and Alternaria leaf spot are the documented agents on dill.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi, chiefly Cercosporidium punctum (Cercospora blight) and Alternaria spp., spread by splash, wind, and infected seed and favored by warm, wet weather and overhead irrigation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from the carrot family, and remove infected debris; there is no effective home-garden cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungi over.

diseases.name: Damping-off and seedling rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting dill seed sits a long time before emerging.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where dill's slow germination leaves seed sitting in the danger zone.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows dill's already slow germination favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed.
